# OneCoin/Cryptoqueen: Evidence-Bounded Reconstruction

## Scope and evidentiary limits

The returned benchmark evidence consists of two sources:

- [Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) **[SRC-001]**
- [Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) **[SRC-002]**

The excerpts returned by the benchmark are truncated. They do not include the full text of an indictment, complaint, warrant, judgment, or technical investigation. Accordingly, this report distinguishes:

- **Established enforcement facts:** matters directly stated by the DOJ or reported as a sentence or enforcement action.
- **Government allegations:** assertions described as allegations or attributed to the government.
- **Investigative assessments:** enforcement authorities’ descriptions of the scheme or their continuing investigative activity.
- **Unresolved matters:** issues not established by the returned evidence.
- **Omissions:** subjects for which the benchmark supplied no sufficient evidence.

No entity IDs were supplied by the benchmark. Entity names are therefore used only where the sources identify them. No unsupported founder, company, relationship, or technical detail is added.

## Executive summary

The returned evidence describes OneCoin as an international cryptocurrency investment scheme that began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and was based in Sofia. It was marketed and sold through a global multi-level-marketing network. The two documented co-founders are Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

The government’s account, as reported in the returned materials, is that OneCoin made misleading representations concerning the value and technical basis of the purported cryptocurrency. The alleged representations included that OneCoin’s value was determined by market supply and demand and that it operated on a private blockchain capable of identifying coins and recording transactions. The government allegedly maintained that the value was set arbitrarily and that no public, verifiable blockchain existed. [SRC-002]

The sources describe more than $4 billion in worldwide investments and approximately 3.5 million investors in the government’s account. Greenwood is specifically described as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and is alleged to have received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, amounting to more than $300 million. SRC-002 reports that he was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

Ignatova is identified as a co-founder and as a person who, with Greenwood and others, allegedly orchestrated the scheme. The returned evidence does not establish a more specific operational role for her, does not report a conviction or guilty plea, and does not establish her current location, whether she is alive, or whether she has been apprehended. SRC-001 states that the FBI continues to pursue her; SRC-002 says that she remains at large. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

## Origins and documented beginning

### Operations in Bulgaria

The sources place the beginning of OneCoin’s operations in 2014:

- SRC-001 states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria.
- SRC-002 states that OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014.

The evidence therefore supports the following limited conclusion:

> OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and was based in Sofia.

The sources do not establish:

- the precise date of commencement;
- the legal incorporation date of OneCoin Ltd.;
- the location or circumstances of the founders’ first meeting;
- the founders’ pre-OneCoin activities;
- the origin of the name “OneCoin”;
- the existence of a founding agreement; or
- whether any person other than Ignatova and Greenwood was involved in founding the enterprise.

### Entry into the United States

SRC-002 states that OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The returned evidence does not provide a more precise date, identify the first U.S. distributor or entity, or describe the initial U.S. marketing structure.

## Principal founders and documented roles

### Ruja Ignatova

#### Established identification

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. SRC-002 likewise identifies her as OneCoin’s other co-founder in relation to Greenwood. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

The DOJ further states that Ignatova, Greenwood, and others orchestrated a large international cryptocurrency investment scheme. This is an enforcement description and government characterization of the alleged conduct, not a substitute for a reproduced conviction or judgment against Ignatova. [SRC-001]

#### Role supported by the evidence

The returned evidence supports identifying Ignatova as:

- a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd.; and
- one of the people whom the DOJ says orchestrated the international investment scheme.

The sources do **not** provide a specific operational title or independently documented function for her, such as chief executive, technical architect, marketing director, or financial controller. Those descriptions are omitted rather than inferred.

#### Legal status in the returned evidence

The sources identify Ignatova as a fugitive or person at large:

- SRC-001 describes her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and states that the FBI continues to pursue her.
- SRC-002 states that she was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022 and remains at large.

The returned material does not include:

- the text of an indictment;
- a criminal complaint;
- an arrest warrant;
- specific charges;
- a conviction;
- a guilty plea;
- a trial outcome; or
- a sentencing record concerning Ignatova.

Accordingly, the evidence supports describing the allegations and enforcement pursuit, but not stating that Ignatova has been convicted.

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

#### Founder status

The DOJ identifies Karl Sebastian Greenwood as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. SRC-002 describes him as a co-founder of the cryptocurrency OneCoin. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

#### Distribution role

SRC-002 describes Greenwood as OneCoin’s “top MLM distributor.” It also reports the government’s allegation that he earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million. These are specific allegations or reported prosecution facts in the returned source and should not be expanded into unsupported claims about the complete compensation system. [SRC-002]

#### Representations attributed to Greenwood

According to the government’s allegations summarized by SRC-002, Greenwood represented that:

- OneCoin’s value was based on market supply and demand; and
- OneCoin had a private blockchain that identified OneCoins and recorded historical transactions.

The same source reports the government’s position that OneCoin’s value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces and that no public, verifiable blockchain existed. These technical and valuation propositions are presented in the returned evidence as government allegations summarized by a secondary source. [SRC-002]

#### Sentence and forfeiture

SRC-002 reports that Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. The excerpt does not supply:

- the sentencing date;
- the underlying judgment;
- the counts of conviction;
- the plea or trial history; or
- the legal basis for the forfeiture amount.

The sentence itself is therefore a reported enforcement fact, while the underlying legal details remain omitted from the returned evidence.

### Other founders

The returned benchmark evidence does not establish any additional founder. In particular, although the research queries considered Konstantin Ignatov, the returned sources do not identify him as a founder or document his role in the scheme.

The evidence therefore supports naming only:

1. Ruja Ignatova; and
2. Karl Sebastian Greenwood.

## Operating model

### Marketing and sale of the purported cryptocurrency

The sources describe OneCoin as a cryptocurrency of the same name that was marketed and sold through a global MLM network. The DOJ characterizes it as a fraudulent cryptocurrency and an international investment scheme. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

The evidence supports the following high-level model:

1. OneCoin was presented to prospective purchasers as a cryptocurrency.
2. Sales occurred through a global multi-level-marketing structure.
3. Members allegedly received commissions for recruiting other purchasers.
4. The government alleged that material representations about value and blockchain functionality were false or misleading.
5. Victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide, according to the DOJ’s account.

### Cryptocurrency packages and recruitment

SRC-002 states that OneCoin members received commissions for recruiting others to purchase “cryptocurrency packages.” This establishes a connection between package sales and recruitment-based compensation. [SRC-002]

The benchmark does not establish:

- the contents of the packages;
- package names or levels;
- package prices;
- the amount of cryptocurrency or tokens associated with each package;
- whether the packages contained educational materials;
- the specific commission percentages for different levels of distributors;
- the identity of regional distributors; or
- whether commissions were paid in fiat currency, OneCoin, or another instrument.

References to educational packages, token allocations, “mining,” or package conversion mechanics would therefore exceed the returned evidence.

### Valuation allegations

The government’s allegations, as summarized in SRC-002, concerned OneCoin’s claimed valuation:

- OneCoin allegedly represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand.
- The government allegedly stated that the value was instead set arbitrarily without regard to market forces.

This is a documented allegation about the valuation model. The returned sources do not provide a transaction-level analysis, internal pricing records, or a judicial finding explaining the complete pricing process. [SRC-002]

### Blockchain allegations

The government allegedly maintained that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain for identifying coins and recording historical transactions. The government’s position, as reported in SRC-002, was that no public, verifiable blockchain actually existed. [SRC-002]

The evidence does not establish the full technical architecture of OneCoin. It does not describe:

- a consensus mechanism;
- a mining algorithm;
- mining hardware;
- mining pools;
- block production;
- token-to-coin conversion;
- wallet architecture;
- a public ledger;
- transaction validation; or
- whether any private database or internal ledger existed in a particular form.

The supported conclusion is narrower: the government alleged that OneCoin’s blockchain representation was false or misleading and that no public, verifiable blockchain existed.

## Promotion, recruitment, and distribution network

### Global MLM structure

Both sources describe OneCoin’s distribution as global or international. The DOJ states that the cryptocurrency was marketed and sold through a global MLM network. SRC-002 states that members received commissions for recruiting others to buy cryptocurrency packages. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

This supports a distribution structure in which:

- sales were conducted through network participants;
- recruitment was economically incentivized;
- members could receive commissions for bringing in additional purchasers; and
- the operation reached investors internationally.

### Greenwood’s place in the network

Greenwood is specifically described as the top MLM distributor. SRC-002 further reports the allegation that he received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales and earned more than $300 million. [SRC-002]

The returned evidence does not identify the complete hierarchy below or alongside Greenwood. It does not establish:

- the names of other senior distributors;
- national or regional leadership structures;
- individual recruitment events;
- sales scripts;
- promotional conferences;
- country-by-country sales totals;
- the full compensation plan; or
- the identities of all participants.

### Geographic reach

The documented geographic facts are limited to:

- Bulgaria: operations began there in 2014.
- Sofia, Bulgaria: OneCoin was based there.
- United States: operations began there around 2015.
- Global or international reach: the sources describe the scheme and its victims in those terms.
- Sweden and the United Kingdom: SRC-002 describes Greenwood as a citizen of both countries.

The evidence does not provide a complete list of operating countries, victim countries, distributor countries, or associated corporate jurisdictions.

## Associated individuals and entities

### Individuals involved in the alleged scheme

The returned evidence identifies:

- **Ruja Ignatova:** co-founder of OneCoin Ltd.; described by the DOJ as one of the people who orchestrated the alleged scheme.
- **Karl Sebastian Greenwood:** co-founder; top MLM distributor; associated with the alleged valuation and blockchain representations; reported as sentenced to 20 years in prison.

No other individual is established by the returned evidence as a participant in OneCoin’s operations.

### Enforcement and administrative officials

SRC-001 identifies several officials in connection with enforcement or compensation activity:

- James C. Barnacle Jr., Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office;
- Jenifer L. Piovesan, Special Agent in Charge of IRS Criminal Investigation;
- Jay Clayton, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York;
- A. Tysen Duva, Assistant Attorney General of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division; and
- Drew Halter, an MNF Attorney Advisor leading the remission process.

The sources do not identify these officials as participants in OneCoin. Their association is with investigation, prosecution, enforcement statements, forfeiture, or victim compensation.

### Entities

The returned evidence identifies or associates the following entities:

- **OneCoin Ltd.:** the company identified as associated with OneCoin and based in Sofia, Bulgaria.
- **OneCoin:** the name used for the purported cryptocurrency and the associated scheme.
- **FBI:** involved in the criminal fraud investigation and continuing pursuit of Ignatova.
- **IRS Criminal Investigation:** involved in the criminal fraud investigation.
- **U.S. Department of Justice:** announced the compensation process and described the enforcement position.
- **Southern District of New York:** handled a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions.
- **Justice Department Office of International Affairs:** provided significant assistance.
- **Justice Department Criminal Division Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section:** manages the remission process.
- **Kroll Settlement Administration LLC:** serves as remission administrator.

The sources do not establish a complete corporate network, the ownership of every associated company, or the legal relationships among all entities.

## Investor amounts, losses, and forfeiture

The sources use slightly different formulations:

- SRC-001 states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency.
- SRC-002 describes the matter as a $4 billion fraud scheme and states that the government charged Greenwood and others with securing more than $4 billion from approximately 3.5 million investors.

These figures are broadly consistent, but the returned sources do not explain whether they represent gross sales, investor deposits, alleged losses, or another measure. The report therefore preserves the sources’ formulations rather than treating them as a single precisely defined accounting figure. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

SRC-001 states that more than $40 million in forfeited assets were available for victim compensation. The DOJ announced a remission process for eligible victims who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC was identified as the remission administrator. [SRC-001]

The sources do not establish:

- the total amount ultimately recovered;
- the number of eligible claims;
- the amount payable to each claimant;
- the distribution date;
- the complete asset inventory; or
- whether all victims will be compensated.

## Timeline

### 2014: commencement in Bulgaria

OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and was based in Sofia. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### Around 2015: U.S. operations

OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The returned source does not provide a more precise date or describe the entry mechanism. [SRC-002]

### 2014–2019: documented investment period

The DOJ identifies 2014 through 2019 as the period relevant to purchases of the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency for purposes of the remission process. The DOJ also describes victims as investing more than $4 billion worldwide during the scheme. [SRC-001]

### June 2022: FBI Most Wanted designation

SRC-002 states that Ruja Ignatova was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. [SRC-002]

### September 15, 2023: reported Greenwood sentence

SRC-002, published on September 15, 2023, reports that Greenwood had been sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. The source does not state the sentencing date. [SRC-002]

### April 13, 2026: remission announcement

On April 13, 2026, the DOJ announced a compensation process for OneCoin victims using forfeited assets. The DOJ stated that more than $40 million was available for victim compensation and identified Kroll Settlement Administration LLC as the remission administrator. [SRC-001]

SRC-001 also states that the petition deadline was June 30, but the returned excerpt does not specify the year of that deadline.

### Latest status in the returned evidence

The latest returned evidence states that:

- Ignatova remains at large;
- the FBI continues to pursue her; and
- she is described as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive.

The evidence does not establish her current physical location or physical condition. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

## Ruja Ignatova: established facts and unresolved claims

### Established enforcement facts

The following are supported by the returned sources:

- Ignatova is identified as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. [SRC-001; SRC-002]
- The DOJ describes her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. [SRC-001]
- SRC-002 states that she was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. [SRC-002]
- SRC-002 states that she remains at large. [SRC-002]
- The DOJ states that the FBI continues to pursue her. [SRC-001]

### Government allegations

The DOJ states that Ignatova, Greenwood, and others orchestrated an international cryptocurrency investment scheme that defrauded investors around the world. The returned evidence does not reproduce the underlying charging document or identify the specific criminal counts against her. [SRC-001]

The allegation should therefore be reported as a government enforcement account, not as a conviction established by the returned materials.

### Unresolved status questions

The benchmark evidence does not establish:

- whether Ignatova is alive;
- where she is located;
- whether she has been secretly protected;
- whether she has been apprehended;
- whether she has died;
- whether any particular account of her disappearance is accurate; or
- whether the FBI designation remains current beyond the dates reported by the sources.

No disputed account about her whereabouts was returned by the benchmark. The appropriate conclusion is that her status is unresolved beyond the sources’ statements that she remains at large and is being pursued.

## Evidence classification

| Subject | Classification supported by the returned evidence |
|---|---|
| OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 | Directly stated by the sources |
| OneCoin was based in Sofia | Directly stated by SRC-001 |
| Ignatova and Greenwood were co-founders | Directly stated by the sources |
| OneCoin used a global MLM network | DOJ description and source reporting |
| Commissions were paid for recruiting purchasers | Government allegation summarized by SRC-002 |
| OneCoin’s valuation was allegedly set arbitrarily | Government allegation summarized by SRC-002 |
| No public, verifiable blockchain existed | Government allegation summarized by SRC-002 |
| Greenwood was the top MLM distributor | Reported description in SRC-002 |
| Greenwood received 5% of monthly sales and more than $300 million | Reported allegation in SRC-002 |
| Greenwood received a 20-year sentence | Reported enforcement fact in SRC-002 |
| Ignatova remains at large | Statement in SRC-002 |
| FBI continues pursuing Ignatova | DOJ enforcement statement in SRC-001 |
| Ignatova’s location, survival, or apprehension | Not established |
| Detailed package, token, mining, and blockchain mechanics | Not established |
| Complete list of founders and distributors | Not established |

## Contradictions, tensions, and omissions

### Loss-amount formulation

SRC-001 refers to more than $4 billion invested worldwide. SRC-002 uses both “$4 billion fraud scheme” and “over $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors.” The amounts are broadly compatible, but the sources do not define the accounting basis for each formulation. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### Greenwood’s sentence

SRC-002 reports a 20-year sentence but does not provide the judgment, counts, sentencing date, or underlying record. The sentence is reported, but its legal details cannot be reconstructed from the returned evidence alone. [SRC-002]

### Other sentenced participants

SRC-001 states that several key figures have been sentenced, but the returned excerpt does not identify all of them. Greenwood is the only sentenced participant specifically documented in the returned materials. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### Remission deadline

SRC-001 states that the petition deadline was June 30 but does not state the year. Because the announcement is dated April 13, 2026, the year may be contextually apparent, but it is not specified in the returned excerpt and should not be treated as independently established. [SRC-001]

### Ignatova’s status terminology

SRC-002 says Ignatova remains at large. SRC-001 calls her an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and states that the FBI continues to pursue her. These descriptions are not necessarily inconsistent, but neither source establishes why she remains at large or provides a current location. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### Technical and operational gaps

The returned evidence does not support a detailed reconstruction of:

- educational-package contents;
- package pricing or levels;
- token allocation;
- mining;
- coin conversion;
- technical ledger architecture;
- specific recruitment events;
- the full commission hierarchy;
- regional distributors;
- complete corporate ownership;
- all countries of operation; or
- the full chronology of enforcement events.

## Conclusion

The benchmark evidence supports a careful, limited reconstruction of OneCoin as a Bulgaria-based, internationally distributed MLM cryptocurrency investment scheme that began operating in 2014. It identifies Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as the documented co-founders. Greenwood’s documented role is more specific: he was described as the top MLM distributor and was associated with alleged representations about OneCoin’s value and blockchain. Ignatova’s documented role is limited to co-founder status and the DOJ’s allegation that she helped orchestrate the scheme.

The evidence supports reporting the government’s allegations concerning arbitrary valuation, the absence of a public verifiable blockchain, recruitment commissions, and more than $4 billion in investments. It does not support filling in the missing technical, package, distribution, or corporate details.

For Ignatova, the established position in the returned evidence is that she is identified as a co-founder, was placed on the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022, remains at large according to SRC-002, and continues to be pursued according to SRC-001. Her location, physical condition, apprehension, and the truth of any unreturned account about her disappearance remain unresolved.
